title: The smaller plate
text:
Ivo tried three diets in two years. Each one worked for a few weeks and then stopped, usually around the time something went wrong at work.

The fourth attempt was different, mostly because it was smaller.

His doctor didn't give him a plan. She asked one question: what do you actually eat on a normal Tuesday? He wrote it down for a week and brought the list back.

Nothing on it was shocking. The problem was quantity, not quality. His portion sizes had grown slowly over ten years, and he had never noticed because the plate was always full.

They changed two things. He used a smaller plate, and he stopped eating in front of the television, where he could finish a meal without remembering it.

No food was banned. He still ate bread, still had a takeaway on Fridays.

Seven months later he had lost nine kilos, and more importantly he had not thought about a diet since March.

He describes it now in one sentence: he didn't get more disciplined, he just made the sensible thing easier than the other thing.

questions.q: Why did the earlier diets fail?
options: They stopped working when life got stressful
He was allergic to the ingredients

questions.q: What was the real problem with his eating?
What two changes did he make?
options: A smaller plate and no eating in front of the TV

questions.q: How does he explain his success?
options: He made the sensible choice the easier one
He found a better diet plan
He started going to the gym

title: Reading the label backwards
text:
The yoghurt was marketed as a healthy breakfast. Low-fat, high in protein, a picture of fruit on the front.

A nutritionist visiting the school held it up and asked the class to guess the sugar content. The answers ranged from four grams to ten. The real number was 21 grams per pot, more than a standard chocolate bar.

Her point was not that yoghurt is bad. It was that the front of a package is advertising, and the back is information.

She taught them one habit. Ignore the claims on the front completely. Turn the pack over, find the per-100-gram column, and read three lines: sugar, saturated fat, salt. Then look at the ingredients, which are listed in order of quantity. If sugar appears in the first three, you know what you're buying.

One student tested it that evening on eight products in her kitchen. Six were fine. Two were not what she thought, and one of them was the cereal she gave her children every morning.

She didn't throw it away. She moved it to Sundays.

questions.q: How much sugar did the yoghurt contain?
What was the nutritionist's main point?
options: The front is advertising, the back is information

questions.q: What three lines did she say to check?
What did the student do with the cereal?
options: Kept it but moved it to Sundays
